title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent-to-Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether inserting a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations during intent→device-configuration translation. Using a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and gpt-5-mini as the generator, we executed the preregistered paired confirmatory comparison under shared-initial-candidate semantics (one generated candidate reused across arms; at most one bounded repair allowed). All 240 pairs completed without infrastructure/model failures. Every candidate passed the deterministic validator in both arms (n11 = 240; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). No repairs were applied because the shared initial candidate already satisfied verifier predicates for every task. We (1) present the preregistered design and the artifact-backed execution accounting, (2) explain why the preregistered shared-generation semantics produced a null confirmatory result in this setting, (3) document a prespecified comparison (GVR vs schema-constrained baseline) that the archived run did not execute, and (4) outline reproducible next steps (independent per-condition generation, adversarial tasks, multi-model evaluation, stronger semantic/formal verifiers) required to evaluate operational reliability of agentic NetOps pipelines.

sections.introduction: LLM-based intent-to-configuration automation promises operational efficiency but raises safety concerns because stochastic generators can fabricate commands or violate semantic invariants (reachability, ACLs, workflow safety). Prior work therefore advocates generate–validate–repair patterns and deterministic validators as mitigation layers. We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment to answer the question: Under a preregistered shared-generation design, does a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (GVR) reduce verifier-detected semantic-violation rates relative to a strong unconstrained baseline when translating natural-language intents into device configurations? Our contributions: (i) a frozen preregistration and fully archived execution/analysis of a paired experiment on a public synthetic NetOps task bank (240 pairs); (ii) artifact-grounded confirmatory statistics showing a null effect under shared-generation semantics; and (iii) a diagnostic reconciliation connecting preregistered design choices (notably shared_initial_candidate) to the observed null result and prescriptive, reproducible follow-ups.
sections.related_work: LLM hallucinations and faulty code/tool outputs motivate validator-interposed architectures in many domains. Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) has improved mechanically checkable outcomes (compilation, test-passing) in prior studies but domain-level semantic guarantees for network policies remain unresolved. Schema/grammar-constrained decoding raises syntactic correctness rates but does not guarantee semantic invariants such as reachability or ACL preservation. Recent NetOps prototypes and intent-translation systems embed validators and human oversight, yet controlled preregistered paired tests of GVR versus strong baselines—particularly under clearly specified generation semantics—are scarce; this experiment addresses that gap with an explicit estimand and archived artifacts.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand: The preregistration (study_id c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1; archived prior to execution) defined a confirmatory paired estimand: the paired difference in verifier-detected semantic-violation rate (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The public synthetic task bank contained 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks = 240 tasks; each task includes initial device state, intent, workflow/safety constraints, and an expected final state. Model and tools: generator requested = gpt-5-mini; deterministic verifier = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Execution contract (frozen): adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, execution_mode = scientific_confirmatory, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, independent_condition_generation = false, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, planned_episode_count = 480 (240 tasks × 2 scored conditions). Repair policy: at most one bounded LLM-guided repair per task (explicit edit budget documented in preregistration). Statistical plan: two prespecified primary comparisons (C vs A and C vs B) with Bonferroni correction (family alpha = 0.05 → per-comparison alpha = 0.025); primary analysis implemented as an exact McNemar two-sided test and paired-bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Prespecified comparisons and execution status: (1) C vs A (GVR vs unconstrained baseline) — executed and analyzed (see Results); (2) C vs B (GVR vs schema-constrained baseline) — prespecified in the preregistration but not executed in the archived run (artifacts lack a recorded rationale). Reproducibility: execution artifacts (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) are authoritative for all reported numeric values and accounting; these artifact paths are included in the archival manifest.
sections.results: Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation (artifact-backed): planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240. The shared-initial-candidate design produced one model call per task whose output was scored in both arms; archived provider-call accounting shows stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 240} (deterministic reconciliation artifact: analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). Confirmatory contingency counts (artifact-backed): n11 = 240 (both arms accepted), n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Paired estimate and inference (archived analysis/results.json): rate_GVR − rate_baseline = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Repair application: repair_applied = false for all episodes because the shared initial candidate satisfied the verifier predicates in every task (see representative scoring artifacts under execution/scoring/ and execution/responses/). Missingness and exclusions: complete_pairs = 240; failed episodes = 0; no exclusions applied (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Secondary/sensitivity artifacts (cluster stratifications, contamination checks, conservative failure-as-violation sensitivity) are archived and do not change the primary null outcome.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The preregistered null confirmatory result is artifact-grounded: under the archived shared_initial_candidate semantics the generator produced verifier-compliant configurations for every task and therefore the bounded repair stage was never invoked; consequently GVR provided no additional verifier-detected benefit over the unconstrained baseline in this run. Two artifact-backed, non-exclusive explanations account for the null result: (1) task/verifier match — the synthetic task bank and the verifier predicates created a distribution the generator could satisfy reliably under the supplied prompting, and (2) sensitivity reduction due to shared-generation semantics — reusing a single initial generation across arms prevents per-condition stochastic differences that GVR might exploit when generation varies between arms. Design and statistical implications: the preregistered decision to use shared_initial_candidate (documented in the execution contract and model_configuration.json) reduced model-call cost and guaranteed input parity across arms but also reduced sensitivity to detect interventions that rely on independent stochastic variation. Multiplicity handling: a Bonferroni plan for two prespecified primary comparisons was preregistered; because only one prespecified comparison (C vs A) was executed in the archived run, multiplicity correction was not applied to the reported p-value; the analysis executor produced the exact McNemar p and bootstrap CI archived at analysis/results.json. Procedural limitation (artifact-backed): the prespecified comparison C vs B (GVR vs schema-constrained baseline) from the preregistration was not executed; execution artifacts do not contain a recorded rationale for this omission and we therefore report it as an unresolved procedural limitation. Operational implications and recommended reproducible follow-ups (all consistent with preregistered planned outputs): (i) rerun with independent per-condition generation so each arm receives an independently sampled candidate (remove shared_initial_candidate) to allow repair paths to trigger, (ii) inject adversarial/golden tasks explicitly designed to violate verifier predicates to measure repair utilization, (iii) evaluate multiple generator families and prompt variants to assess cross-model robustness, and (iv) integrate stronger semantic/formal verifiers (e.g., SMT or constraint hybrids) to widen oracle coverage. These next steps match the preregistration’s unresolved questions and planned outputs and are required before generalizing about GVR’s operational benefits.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment testing GVR on a synthetic intent-to-configuration NetOps task bank. Under preregistered shared-initial-candidate semantics, every initial generated candidate passed the deterministic validator in both baseline and guarded arms (n = 240 pairs), yielding a null confirmatory result: GVR did not reduce verifier-detected semantic-violation rates in this run (paired estimate = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.00; 95% CI [0.0, 0.0]). The artifact manifests and deterministic reconciliation are authoritative for these numbers. The result demonstrates that (a) when generator+prompting already satisfy verifier predicates on a task distribution, GVR may be redundant for those predicates, and (b) to evaluate GVR’s operational value one must run independent-generation, adversarial, and multi-model experiments and adopt stronger semantic or formal verifiers to measure residual risks not captured by the current oracle.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
